mappings.note: Both limbs turn on the sign and size of the two charges - beads negative, clay positive - and on the equality that makes an atom neutral. That is LO-1's 'based on their charge'. Not LO-3: no term (atomic number, isotope, valency) is being defined; not LO-4: nothing is counted from A and Z.

Same outcome as P1 but the other half of it: the analogy is judged on WHERE the electrons sit - discrete seeds inside a continuous positive mass - which is LO-1's 'position in the atom'. P1 is the charge clause, this is the position clause; I did not invent a separate code for the analogy. Not LO-28: its one usable clause is about labelled DIAGRAMS of atomic models and nothing is drawn here (I cite LO-28 only at S57).

PARTIAL FIT. The graded point is that the same light, negatively charged particle comes off every cathode, i.e. the electron is a universal constituent. LO-1 covers its charge and its being one of the three subatomic particles; nothing in curriculum 82 covers discovery evidence or universality, so this is the nearest legal code, not a clean one.

The whole counterfactual runs off the sign of the nuclear charge: a negative probe is attracted where alpha is repelled. Charge of the subatomic particles plus the nucleus's position - LO-1. Not LO-2: no shell or energy level enters the answer.

The argument is that mass and positive charge must be concentrated, not spread (LO-1, position clause). CG7 is added because the point being graded is that one result killed a standing model - 'Science is ever evolving'. I cite CG7 only where supersession is the thing being graded (here, and N5), not merely mentioned (N1).

The student is asked to POSE a question about what went on inside the atom and inside Rutherford's head - literally C-7.2-LO-2 ('pose question ... is it possible to understand everything that happens completely inside an atom?'). Every other gold-foil item in this batch asks the student to answer a question; this is the only one that asks them to raise one.

Both A and R are statements about where mass and positive charge sit (concentrated nucleus vs uniform sphere), so the item is graded on LO-1's position clause. No CG7: it tests whether R explains A, not that the model was superseded.

No real element is recalled - an invented symbol has to obey the IUPAC writing rule (first letter capital, second lower case). That is the notation convention, C-1.1-LO-6 ('use scientific conventions as per international [standards]'). Not C-1.3-LO-2, which I reserve for recalling the actual symbols of the first eighteen elements.

Same outcome as P8, honestly so: it is the other side of the same convention - P8 applies the rule, this one argues why a single international standard has to exist at all. There is no legal code for scientific communication, so I did not split the pair artificially.
Textbook LO-4: e, p and n produced from Z = 26 and A = 56. Pure arithmetic on the standard relations, no term defined and no notation to decode, so not LO-3 and not LO-6.

LO-4 again, one step of it: n = A - Z. Shares an outcome with P10 because it is the same calculation with one output instead of three - within this family the variable is which quantity is unknown, not which outcome applies.

LO-4 run backwards: the mass number is the unknown, built from Z + n. LO-4 names only 'electrons, protons and neutrons' as the things calculated, so this is the nearest legal code rather than an exact one; LO-3 would be for explaining what a mass number is, which the item does not ask.

Differs from P10-P12 by the route in: the datum arrives in standard mass-number notation, so the superscript must be read as A (LO-6, scientific convention) before the proton count can be inferred from the 11 electrons and n = 23 - 11 taken (LO-4). The other three numericals hand over Z and A in words and need no notation.

Two steps: build 2,4 / 2,7 / 2,8,4 by the shell-filling rule (LO-2) and then read the outermost shell off it, which is the valence-electron idea (LO-3). P15 stops at the first step and gets LO-2 alone - that is the split in this family.
Distribution over K, L, M and nothing else - LO-2 word for word. No valence reading, no valency and no element identified, so LO-3 and LO-5 stay out.

The riddle is a classification task: A = 23, Z = 11 and 'soft metal, reacts with water' have to be read together to name sodium - LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify elements accurately'. LO-4 carries the small second ask, 23 - 11 = 12 neutrons. Not LO-3: nothing is defined.

The verdict asked for is the word 'isotopes' and why identical Z forces same-element (LO-3). LO-4 is cited because the comparison genuinely requires producing A = 23 and A = 24 first. Not LO-5: the element need not be classified from the data, only the relation between the two atoms named.

POOR FIT on the calculation. Abundance-weighted average atomic mass is not stated by any outcome - LO-4 covers only counting e, p and n. LO-3 supplies the two concepts in play ('atomic mass', 'isotopes') and LO-5 the 'interpret data, such as atomic mass' clause, which is the closest curriculum 82 comes to a weighted average.

Each of the four claims is judged on what the scattering evidence says about the location of mass, positive charge, neutrons and electrons - LO-1's position clause, four times over. No CG7 even though option (ii) mentions the plum pudding model: the item grades what the experiment does and does not show, not that science moved on.

All four statements test that energy levels are discrete and that electrons are confined to them, which is the substance of LO-2. LO-2 does not state the no-radiation postulate, so C1.1 is cited alongside it as the only intact row that names Bohr's model - the row that names the models properly, LO-28, is a shredded fusion (see report).

Needs both isotopes and isobars named from LO-3, and unlike P17 the data arrive as a three-row table that must be worked (A of Z = 37, A of X = 37) before either relation appears - LO-5's 'interpret data ... to classify'. P17 gets LO-4 for its arithmetic; here the work is table interpretation, so LO-5.

The cleanest LO-1 in the batch: the question names its two targets as 'position and characteristics of the positively charged part'. The answer is location (tiny central nucleus) plus charge and mass - exactly LO-1.

POOR FIT. Ordering Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr tests the historical development of the models, and no learning outcome in curriculum 82 states that. CG7's 'Science is ever evolving' is the only text the item actually matches; C1.1 is added as the one intact row naming Bohr's model. LO-28 names Thomson's and Rutherford's models but only inside a diagram clause, and nothing is drawn here, so it does not reach this item either.

The answer is the electrostatic attraction between a negative electron and a positive nucleus - the charges of two subatomic particles and their relative positions, LO-1. Deliberately not LO-2 like N2: no shell, orbit energy or configuration is required, so the Bohr family splits here.

R is the p = e equality in a neutral atom and A is that the three particles were found - both LO-1 content, and the grading turns on whether the particle count explains the structural insight. Same outcome as P1, honestly: both are the neutrality relation.
